issues.title: Rising Property Taxes & Village Debt
issues.status_label: FY2026-27 adopted — structural debt debate ongoing
issues.description:
Village of Pelham adopted {{fact:village-budget-fy2627}} FY2026-27 budget — {{fact:village-budget-increase-fy2627}} increase overriding the state tax cap. Village debt grew from {{fact:village-debt-2021}} in 2021 to {{fact:village-debt-2026}} by early 2026. Fiscal management has been a major focus of the November 2026 election, and the cost of the flood mitigation project is now the center of an ongoing debate between the candidates. Neighborhood Party candidates (September 30 statement) project Village debt of about $53.7M: the $48.5M project cost they cite, plus 10% for future overruns, less about $17.6M in expected county, state and FEMA grants, plus roughly $18M of existing debt. They say it could be much higher if the earmarks fall through. Incumbent trustees Russell Solomon and Krystal Howell (October 2 response) say no bond has been authorized to build the project, that the roughly $48.5M figure is an engineering estimate that will keep changing as the design develops, and that the Village is pursuing every source of outside funding to reduce the cost to taxpayers. Both are campaign statements, not Village figures, and neither has been independently verified.

NYS Comptroller fiscal stress score: The New York State Comptroller’s office has published fiscal 2025 fiscal stress scores for New York municipalities. Neighborhood Party candidates Anzilotti, Long and Speros (October 5 statement) report that the Village of Pelham scored 19.2, up from 3.3 in fiscal 2024 — the worst score of any Westchester village and the second worst of all Westchester municipalities, behind only Yonkers — while Pelham Manor, Ardsley, Bronxville, Irvington and Larchmont scored between 1.7 and 3.3. They say the largest component of the Village’s score is the ratio of its general fund to its annual spending, and point to the September 22 purchase of an Avant 640i loader from the contingency budget line, in anticipation of future revenue the Village expected to receive. They also say growth in that contingency line (at most $320,000 in budgets since 2019, over $780,000 for FY2026-27), together with increased debt service — including on almost $1 million in debt for Municipal Center furniture and window treatments — is what made the Village break the tax cap this year. These figures come from a candidate press release, which the Examiner publishes as received; this site has not independently verified them. The Comptroller’s data shows the Village of Pelham’s fiscal 2025 stress score as 19.2 with a designation of ‘No Designation’ — meaning the Village does not meet the threshold for a formal fiscal stress classification despite the elevated score.

Neighborhood Party alternative flood mitigation plan (October 27, 2026 press release, Anzilotti, Long and Speros): the three NP candidates for Village of Pelham Trustee say their difference with the current board is over how flooding should be mitigated, not whether. Under what they call conservative assumptions, and allowing for no other capital projects, they say the current plan could grow annual debt service from a little over $1.6M to over $4M by FY2034-35, an increase of up to 36% in Village property taxes by 2035, widening the gap between Village of Pelham and Pelham Manor village taxes from 22.5% to about 36%. Their example: a $1M home’s Village of Pelham tax bill rising from $6,915 to $9,405, against a projected $6,927 Pelham Manor bill in 2035. They propose that the board evaluate: (1) eliminating the planned retention tank and pumping station at Julianne’s and instead working with Westchester County and New Rochelle to explore a retention tank on the New Rochelle side of the border, which they estimate would cut about 50% of the project’s cost and remove the need for what they call a divisive eminent domain action that, under the current resolution, must begin by September 2027; (2) more fully accounting for New Rochelle’s stormwater contribution to North Pelham flooding and sharing costs with New Rochelle; (3) a consistent 25-year storm standard in both watersheds, instead of the current 50-year (Highbrook) and 100-year (North Pelham) standards; (4) re-installing a valve on Glenwood Lake to allow controlled drawdown ahead of storms; and (5) phasing the project to limit the budget impact. All figures and characterizations are the candidates’ own.

issues.title: November 2026 — First Contested Village Race Since 2019
issues.description: Three contested races: Village of Pelham trustees (Democrats vs. Neighborhood Party/Republican challengers), Village of Pelham Manor trustees (two seats), and Town Supervisor and Clerk (Mohan and Miller re-running per new state law). After weeks of negotiations between the candidates, the League of Women Voters has scheduled four candidate debates, {{fact:debates-2026}}: Pelham Manor trustees {{fact:debate-manor-trustees.short}}; Town Clerk {{fact:debate-town-clerk.short}} and Town Supervisor {{fact:debate-town-supervisor.short}}, both at Town Hall; and Village of Pelham trustees {{fact:debate-village-trustees.short}} on Zoom. Residents can submit questions to the League. Details on the Elections page. Ahead of the election, Mark Cardwell — the Democrats’ candidate for Pelham Manor Mayor in 2025 — submitted affidavits to the Westchester County Board of Elections on October 16 claiming “personal knowledge” that 16 people registered to vote in Pelham Manor, most of them at their parents’ homes, did not “reside in the district” at those addresses. Under Board of Elections policy, the challenges were forwarded to the Pelham Manor Police Department, which sent a detective and an officer to each residence to interview the voter or a parent and report back within six days. Several residents were alarmed when the visits began, and two of the voters named publicly disputed Cardwell’s claims. The Town of Pelham Democratic Committee said that no candidate or Committee member had “any involvement in, or advance notice of” the challenges, and that it and its candidates “firmly support every eligible voter’s right to cast a lawful ballot.” Cardwell did not respond immediately to the Examiner’s request for comment. (Pelham Examiner, October 26, 2026) At the Pelham Manor board’s October 26 meeting, the police chief said state election law required the department to verify the challenged registrations in person once the county Board of Elections asked, in a letter village officials said was signed by both elections commissioners; Village Manager Luft said the county could instead have used its own bipartisan staff, but the choice was the county’s. A trustee asked the chief to report at the next meeting on the investigations’ cost to the department, and Mayor Lapey, speaking personally, said she was surprised the evidence in the affidavit was deemed sufficient.

issues.title: Pelham Picture House — Future Still Uncertain
issues.description: MOU with PHP Partners terminated. Developer James Smithmeyer working directly with Picture House. No plan approved. Picture House continues to operate and ran a successful summer film series. Candidate Everitt Speros (Neighborhood Party, October 19 campaign statement) says that last winter the Mayor and board tried to force two longstanding local business owners to sell their land so a developer could build a large residential complex next to and including the Picture House, and that community pressure, not the board’s choice, led them to drop the eminent domain threat. He criticizes exclusive developer agreements and secret “blight studies” made without public input. These are the candidate’s own characterizations. Neighborhood Party candidates Anzilotti, Long and Speros (October 20 press release) say the Pelham Green developer also planned what they call a “monstrosity” for the Picture House site on Wolf’s Lane, and cite the Mayor and board’s effort to force local businesses off that site, together with conditions at Pelham Green on Fifth Avenue, as showing the limits of the Mayor’s development approach. These are the candidates’ own characterizations.

issues.title: Colonial Elementary — AC Interim Fix in Place
issues.status_label: Interim fix in place — full HVAC conversion Summer 2027
issues.description: After parents Ashley Mills and incoming PTA President Concetta Eudicone spoke at the June 24 Board of Ed meeting demanding action, the Colonial, Siwanoy, and Prospect Hill PTAs pledged to raise funds for window AC units. New units were installed in time for the first day of school on September 8, 2026. Full HVAC conversion for all schools is still coming Summer 2027 as part of the {{fact:school-bond-approved}} capital bond approved in May 2025. On October 7 the Board of Education accepted an $8,000 donation from the PTAs for additional air conditioning in the elementary schools.

sources.label: Pelham Examiner — September 2026

last_meeting_update.note: The board accepted the PTAs' $8,000 air conditioning donation and heard that new heating systems at Colonial and Prospect Hill remain on track for summer 2027.

issues.title: EMS Station & Community Church — First Street
issues.status_label: No vote taken · site still undecided as of October 5
issues.description: Proposed EMS station near Post Office draws opposition over pedestrian safety and green space. Community Church of the Pelhams appeared for sale in April 2026 and was raised at a Town Council meeting. At the October 5 2026 Town Council meeting, residents near the post office spoke against the site next to it, citing stop signs, residential streets and an already hard-to-cross road. The board said no decision has been made: the options remain the current station, whose parking lot floods in rain, or the lot next to the post office if it can be acquired for $50,000 and is feasible to build on. The Master Facilities Plan’s issues at the Daronco Town House come first; a grant for the station was not awarded but can be reapplied for; and neighbors will be consulted before any decision. The board also said it never approved a station budget: a May 2024 consultant estimate, first cited at the meeting as $3.6 million and corrected on the record to $2.6 million, was drafted from a previous board’s information and approved by neither board. No vote taken and no alternative site has been confirmed.

issues.title: Receiver of Taxes Vacancy — Appointment or Referendum Under Discussion
issues.status_label: Active — no appointment yet; not taken up at the October 5 meeting
issues.description: Erica Winter, elected Town Receiver of Taxes in November 2025, stepped down after less than a year citing a new professional opportunity. Deputy Receiver Darlene Paolericio assumed her duties and continues to fulfill them. The Town Board made no appointment at its September 14, 2026 meeting and is weighing whether to appoint a replacement or hold a public referendum to make the position permanently appointed rather than elected. A full discussion had been expected at the October meeting, but the vacancy was not discussed at the October 5 Town Council meeting, according to its recording, and no appointment has been made. The Receiver of Taxes is responsible for collecting property tax payments from all Pelham residents.

issues.title: Con Edison Rate Case — Settlement Cuts the Increase
issues.status_label: Settlement reached — awaiting Public Service Commission approval
issues.description: Con Edison filed for a large rate increase and the Village of Pelham joined a consortium of 40 Westchester municipalities opposing it. A settlement has since cut the electric increase to about 2.8% of the total customer bill, down from the 13.4% originally proposed, and the gas increase to about 2%. The agreement is not final: the Public Service Commission holds an evidentiary hearing before issuing a decision.

sources.label: Pelham Examiner

issues.title: Feeney Park — Nightly Illegal Fireworks
issues.description: Residents reported nightly illegal fireworks from Feeney Park, in New Rochelle, through summer 2026, often past 11pm. At the July 14 2026 Village board meeting a resident described calling New Rochelle police up to six times a night against only 12 calls logged in their records since Memorial Day. Trustee Howell committed to increased Pelham PD patrols on the Harman/Store Avenue corridor between 8 and 11pm. Residents can send videos to krystal.howell@pelhamny.gov.

sources.label: Village of Pelham board meeting recording

issues.title: Amtrak Forest Road Corridor Project — Pelham Manor
issues.status_label: Active — three-year corridor project; Village Manager in contact with Amtrak's liaison
issues.description: Raised in public comment at the August 17 2026 Pelham Manor board meeting by resident and volunteer firefighter Josh Casper: flyers were delivered to only some affected households, some phases will run 24/7 with track shutdowns, and Amtrak's representative gave no clear noise threshold or reporting mechanism. Litter from past crews and a rail gate left open were also raised. The corridor project is expected to span three years. Village Manager Luft is to stay in contact with Amtrak's project liaison, and the board directed increased police patrol sweeps plus deployment of the village's mobile spotlight along the corridor.
